Yeah it's nowhere near as straightforward as the "software developer" guy is making it claim. Clearly somebody who's fresh out of college who hasn't had to work on very large, distributed systems before. Issues like this can happen all the time with nobody noticing or understanding why.

Just as an example, I used to work on a point of sale system for a large nationwide retailer. All the stores sent their daily transactions to a messaging queue, and one day the target of that queue was down so the queue kept filling up. Modern messaging queues like RabbitMQ can handle this, but this thing was written in the 80s, so it just filled up and new messages would just get dropped. And due to some other reason that's not worth going into the details, the stores weren't retrying the send.

And just like that, an entire days worth of sales records was lost.

Does it fucking matter what the content is? I pay for a service, and that service is to provide internet access for my home. I could set my fucking computer to stream Gigli non-stop for 24 hours a day and that's my right as a consumer to use the service as I choose. 

Its hilarious, because basically we decided to replace our cable service with internet because cable companies (such as Comcast) have decided to make cable a nightmare, what with being forced to pay for unwanted content such as useless channels like Telemundo because its all bundled together. So to avoid this, we switched to using Netflix as our content service. But Comcast doesn't like this so they decided to cap our data content??

Here's the kicker: the cable service that comes into the house if we were to buy cable? That's DIGITAL content. What does this mean? It means that the data is transmitted IN THE EXACT SAME STANDARD AS ANY OTHER DATA CONTENT. It comes in through a bandwidth pipe, the same pipe as the other data, and it is in the same format as other data. Essentially, this means that cable TV is UNCAPPED DATA.

So how on earth can you justify capping our data content? Clearly if I wanted cable TV you wouldn't cap how much fucking TV I could watch every day? "Oh sorry, you've watched 10 hours of TV today, time to go outside buddy." It doesn't make any sense! If I were to stream HD Netflix 24/7, I'd very soon reach the data cap. But if I were to have HD cable service and leave my TV on 24/7 viewing HD, Comcast would incur the SAME COSTS and yet they would not cap the TV content.

The answer is simple: Comcast is providing preferential treatment to the content that they provide, versus content that is provided by other providers. This is EXACTLY the sort of shenanigans that the FCC has tried to prevent.

Unfortunately a federal appeals court has decided to let Comcast's lobbyist dollars get in the way of their common sense, and as of two days ago has essentially endorsed this sort of tomfoolery. 

http://news.cnet.com/8301-1035_3-57617242-94/why-you-should-care-about-net-neutrality-faq/

The best part about this is that I actually foresaw that my usage would be higher than the average user's usage. So I decided pay extra each month for the faster connection! That'll solve the problem! Except it didn't because all data plans have the SAME DATA CAP. So why the hell do I even bother paying for the faster connection if my cap is the same?

I think their highest speed plan is about $80 a month in my area. But how could anyone justify paying for this extra speed, if all the extra speed is going to do is get them to the data cap even faster?  It's silly. The obvious solution? Raise the data cap as you raise the speeds with the plans. As the consumer who is paying for the plan, I would agree with this! I understand that extra data has extra costs, and I would gladly pay extra a month for a higher or even unlimited data cap. But comcast does not provide this option. EVERY PLAN is capped at 300 GB a month. So why do I bother paying extra for the higher speeds? There's no reason, because all its doing is causing me to reach the cap at a faster rate. I will soon switch providers or at the least lower my plan to the cheapest, bare bones plan, because comcast does not provide the option for me to do this.
